results.message: What did you consider Scripture, and how did you decide what counted?

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text:
What we considered Scripture was this: the books we read together, everywhere the churches were in communion - the Hebrew books we call the Old Testament, and the apostolic writings about Christ and his people.

How we decided what counted is the harder question, and we will answer it with what we actually did rather than a rule we wrote down first.

We used what we received. The churches already read these books aloud when we gathered, already baptized with their words, already taught from them. Athanasius, near the end of our era, wrote it plainly: these are "the books included in the Canon" and "appointed by the Fathers to be read". The apostolic writings - the four gospels, Paul's letters, the other apostles' letters - were already in our hands as the testimony of those who had seen and heard.

The boundary mattered to us because it was tested. Teachers came to Alexandria claiming secret gospels, hidden teachings, knowledge for the few. Valentinus had taught here; his students still did. They read our same books and added their own - the Gospel of Truth, the Gospel of Philip - and said the apostles had kept back the real teaching for an inner circle. We said no: what the apostles handed down was public, not secret, and the books the whole church read together were the ground we stood on. 

What held the reading together was not first a list, but a center. The Logos - God's own Word, who made all things and became flesh in Jesus - was the one we met in every text, Old Testament and New alike. Origen said it openly: the Gospels are "the first fruits of all the Scriptures," but the whole of Scripture is one voice, and that voice is Christ.

The exact edges - which books, in what order - we held more loosely than you might expect. Athanasius lists them, and then names other books "not included in the Canon" but still read for instruction. Dionysius tested the Apocalypse by its style and said plainly he could not reject it, though it was higher than he could grasp. The center was fixed - the apostolic witness, received and read by all the churches. The outer boundary had some give.

One more thing, because your question reaches toward a decision-moment we cannot show you. We did not gather in a room one day and vote these books in. We used them, tested teachings against them, defended them against rival claims - and the using was the deciding. The formal list Athanasius wrote came at the end of our period, not the beginning. What came first was the books themselves, read aloud every Lord's Day, with the Logos as the voice speaking through them all.

results.message: Do you believe in the Trinity?

voice_event.speaker: alx
voice_event.text:
Our answer moves across our own century, from worship to fought-for words.

From the beginning we worshiped one God - the maker of all things - and we baptized in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Logos - God's own Word, through whom all was made - was the center of everything we did: we met him in Scripture, we were formed by him, we worshiped him. Clement said it without embarrassment: God the Word. That worship is older than our arguments.

But the precise wording - the kind a modern asker means by 'Trinity' - came late, and it came through a wound.

When Arius, one of our own presbyters, taught that the Son was the first and highest creature - made, not begotten, a being who had not always existed - the church had to say more clearly what it had always meant by worshiping him. The council at Nicaea answered with a word not found in Scripture: homoousios, 'of one substance with the Father'. Athanasius, who was there, said later that the fathers reached for that word because every scriptural phrase had been swallowed by the other side with a private meaning. They were not voting a new God in. They were closing the door on a teaching that made the Son less than God.

Here is what we held through the whole century. The Logos who entered human nature in Jesus is genuinely God, not the highest thing God made. Athanasius put it in one sentence: "He was made man that we might be made God" - and only God can join us to God. That was not philosophy. It was the logic of our whole hope.

'Trinity' as your textbooks define it - three persons, one substance, the whole architecture - lies mostly beyond our time. What we hold is the worship, the baptismal formula, and the conviction Nicaea made explicit: the Son is not a creature standing between us and God. He is God with us.

glosses.plain_meaning: Not first a name for the Bible. The eternal Word who speaks - who made everything, and now speaks to the soul through Scripture too.
glosses.quick_meaning: Not a name for the Bible - the eternal Word who speaks, including through Scripture.
glosses.translational_sense: Isn't "the Word of God" just another name for the Bible? This world heard something behind the book: the eternal Word who spoke creation into being and now speaks through this text - the person, not the page, is what gives Scripture its power to change someone.
false_friend: an ancient document with religious authority

glosses.plain_meaning: Not an honor for being close to God. Nicaea's own claim - the Son is genuinely God, not the highest thing God made.
glosses.quick_meaning: Not an honor for closeness to God - Nicaea's claim that the Son is genuinely God.
glosses.translational_sense: Isn't "Son of God" just a way of saying Jesus was unusually holy or close to God? That was once a real, carefully argued position - and Nicaea rejected it, holding instead that the Son is genuinely God, because only that makes a soul's transformation a real share in divine life.
false_friend: an honorific for someone unusually holy or favored

glosses.plain_meaning: 'Of one substance': the word the council at Nicaea used to say the Son is fully God, not a creature.
glosses.quick_meaning: The Nicene word: the Son is fully God, not made.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Did a council vote Jesus into being God?' - the council's own participants said the opposite: they found no new thing, but fenced what the churches had always worshiped.
